archetype.name: Super Bowl Contender (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A Shanahan offense that ranks first in net EPA on the strength of the league's cleanest pocket and a run-stuffing front, good enough to win any week if it stops handing the ball and field position back.

report.headline: Football's most efficient team, a little lucky, badly in need of its bye
report.take:
San Francisco is back to the version of itself that ran the league in 2022 and 2023. Net EPA of 0.194 ranks first, the same spot those teams held, and it is a sharp break from 2025, when a 12-5 record rested on an 0.833 one-score win rate and 2.62 wins over expected while the underlying net EPA sat 15th. This year the play matches the record far better. Brock Purdy has started every game, and the offense ranks first in success rate (0.526) and second in EPA per play.

The engine is protection. The line allows pressure on 13.4% of dropbacks, the best rate in football, has given up only 7 sacks, and still leads the league in run success rate (0.511). That keeps Purdy on schedule, and passing EPA of 0.268 per play (3rd) follows. The targets show how Shanahan uses it: George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey are the top two, with Mike Evans third, so the passing game lives over the middle and in the flat. On defense the identity is a wall against the run, -0.205 EPA per rush allowed (2nd) and the fewest explosive runs allowed, paired with a pass defense that is only average (15th) and leaky underneath (short-pass EPA allowed 24th).

What the 6-1 hides: the point differential implies 4.3 wins, the team is perfect in one-score games, and wins over expected sit at 1.68 (4th). The leaks are real. Special teams lose 3.25 EPA a game, 31st in the league. The offense has 10 turnovers for a -3 turnover differential, including four in the loss at Atlanta. The passing game has also gone flat lately: after passing EPA in the low 20s against Miami and Arizona, the last three games came in at -2, 3.7 and 2. That stretch overlaps with Evans, Deebo Samuel and Demarcus Robinson missing time, so injuries explain part of it. Nick Bosa has played only two games.

The bye could hardly be better timed. Evans is expected back, McCaffrey's hamstring is called mild, and Bosa and Samuel have a chance to return. The back half includes Minnesota (6-0, top defense), Seattle's second-ranked defense and Kansas City, but also the 0-6 Chargers, a 2-5 Eagles team and Arizona. A healthy version of this offense is the best in the NFC West by a distance. Expect the close-game coin flips to even out, which costs a game or two against the current pace, not the division.

strengths.title: The league's cleanest pocket
strengths.body: San Francisco allows the lowest pressure rate in football and among the fewest sacks, with time to throw near three seconds. That comes from scheme and the line: the run game's success (first in run success rate) keeps defenses honest and play-action alive. Protection this good has been stable across seven games and is the main reason the pass offense ranks third in EPA.

strengths.title: Staying on schedule every down
strengths.body: A 0.526 success rate leads the league, built on runs that rarely get stuffed (16.7% stuff rate) and short, efficient throws to Kittle and McCaffrey. Rushing EPA is only neutral, so the ground game is about avoiding bad downs rather than big plays. It drives sustained offense and should hold, since it rests on the line and the design, not on chunk plays.

strengths.title: A wall against the run
strengths.body: Opponents lose 0.205 EPA per carry, second best, and the defense allows the fewest explosive runs in the league. The raw rushing yards allowed rank poorly, but that reflects volume from trailing opponents, not efficiency. The front has held up with Bosa playing only twice, which suggests the run defense doesn't depend on one player.

concerns.title: Giving back turnovers and field position
concerns.body: Ten turnovers and a -3 turnover differential undercut an offense this efficient, and special teams cost 3.25 EPA a game, 31st in the league. The Atlanta loss was the clearest case: plenty of yards, four giveaways. Turnover luck tends to swing back, but the special-teams hole is a weekly tax that has shown no sign of closing.

concerns.title: Record runs ahead of the margin
concerns.body: The point differential implies 4.3 wins, not six, and a perfect one-score record won't last. Wins over expected rank fourth. The efficiency says this is a very good team; the record says a great one, and the gap tends to close.

concerns.title: Soft underneath, thin at the back
concerns.body: Short passes against this defense produce EPA that ranks 24th, and backs see a larger share of targets than the league norm. Starting safety Marques Sigle (88% of snaps) is out and corner Upton Stout was only emergency depth against Atlanta. This is a structural weakness that injuries make worse.

trend.note: The first month brought blowouts and huge passing EPA. Since then, results have been close wins or a loss, with passing EPA near zero and turnovers piling up, while the receiver room thinned out. The bye and expected returns of Evans and McCaffrey are the reset point.

nextGame.headline: Rested and healthier, SF hosts a Raiders defense soft underneath
nextGame.body:
San Francisco comes off the bye with 14 days of rest to host a 3-4 Raiders team; the Book has not posted a line yet. Las Vegas scores (26.1 a game, 6th) but allows more (28.1, 29th), and the matchup tilts toward the 49ers on both sides. The Raiders' run game is the worst in football by success rate and yards before contact, which runs straight into San Francisco's second-ranked run defense. Kirk Cousins' passing (9th in EPA) is their only real path, and the 49ers' pass defense is average. On the other side, the Raiders' defense allows the worst short-pass EPA in the league and scores touchdowns against it in the red zone 78.6% of the time. The danger is their pass rush (2nd in pressure rate) and their knack for takeaways (2nd), aimed at a team that has been careless with the ball.

Availability is the big swing for San Francisco. Evans is expected back and McCaffrey's mild hamstring strain is expected to clear after the bye. Bosa and Samuel have a chance to return, while Robinson is on IR with a chance to come back. Sigle is listed out and Stout questionable, which matters against a passing team. For Las Vegas, wideout Jack Bech was designated to return from IR, while Dont'e Thornton and tight end Carter Runyon are on IR.

waysToWin.title: Live in the short middle
waysToWin.body: The Raiders allow the worst short-pass EPA in the league, and tight ends draw an outsized share of targets against them. That is San Francisco's whole passing identity: Kittle and McCaffrey on quick throws, with the run game keeping Purdy on schedule. Long, methodical drives also keep Cousins on the sideline.

waysToWin.title: Make Las Vegas one-dimensional
waysToWin.body: Las Vegas ranks last in run success and yards before contact, and San Francisco's run defense is second in EPA. If early downs go nowhere on the ground, Cousins faces long-yardage passing all day against a defense that still generates pressure on a quarter of dropbacks.

waysToWin.title: Finish drives with touchdowns
waysToWin.body: The Raiders give up touchdowns on 78.6% of red-zone trips, 30th in football. An offense that leads the league in success rate should turn drives into sevens rather than field goals, which also helps offset San Francisco's special-teams deficit.

waysToLose.title: Another turnover-fest
waysToLose.body: Las Vegas has the second-most takeaways in football, and San Francisco has given the ball away 10 times, including four at Atlanta. Short fields and lost possessions are the most likely way an efficiency edge disappears. The Raiders also lead the league in covering spreads, so they keep games closer than their profile suggests.

waysToLose.title: The pass rush wins up front
waysToLose.body: The Raiders' pressure rate ranks second against the league's best pass protection. If they win that matchup, the rhythm passing game that has already stalled for three weeks gets worse, and hits on Purdy are when the ball comes loose.

waysToLose.title: Cousins carves a thin secondary
waysToLose.body: Las Vegas passes efficiently (9th in EPA), and San Francisco's pass defense is only middle of the pack and weak underneath. That is before counting Sigle out and Stout limited. Add the special-teams leak, and a shootout with a few hidden-yardage losses is how this flips.

nextGame.watch: Whether the league's cleanest pocket holds against the Raiders' second-ranked pass rush without the ball coming loose.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency is real. First in net EPA, first in success rate and first in pressure allowed is the profile of a team that has done this before, in 2022 and 2023. The part that will regress is the record's cushion. The perfect one-score mark and nearly two wins over expected won't repeat, and the schedule includes three heavyweights in Minnesota, Seattle's defense and Kansas City. Weaker opponents in Dallas's defense, the winless Chargers, Philadelphia and Arizona leave room to bank wins.

The passing slump looks mostly like a health problem. With Evans back and McCaffrey ready, the passing EPA should move back toward its early-season level, though maybe not the September peaks. The turnover rate should improve with normal luck. Special teams is the piece least likely to fix itself, and the secondary's depth bears watching. The NFC West lead looks safe; the fight is for seeding.
swingFactors: Health of Evans, McCaffrey and Bosa after the bye
Results against MIN, SEA and KC

confidence.note: Seven games, strong efficiency, but a heavy injury list clouds the near term.
